Shrimp scad (Alepes djedaba) attains an ultimate total length of approximately 40.0 centimeters [Li = approximately 40.0 centimeters], a size typical for a fast-growing carangid inhabiting tropical coastal waters. Field surveys along the Indian coastline have documented that puberty, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis in females and active spermatogenesis in males, is reached at a total length of 16.3 centimeters [Lp = 16.3 centimeters]. This relatively small size at sexual maturation suggests that the species can begin reproducing early in its life cycle, a trait that may buffer populations against fishing pressure in regions where it is commercially targeted. The relationship between length and body mass in this species follows a power-law curve derived from extensive morphometric sampling, providing a reliable basis for estimating mass from length data. Individuals transitioning to the juvenile stage after settlement in nearshore habitats undergo a rapid period of allometric growth that continues until they approach their asymptotic size.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], the embryonic development of Alepes djedaba proceeds rapidly, with the yolk-sac larva emerging from the chorion after approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days]. The newly hatched prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during this brief lecithotrophic phase and weighs just 0.0014 grams [Wwb = 0.0014 grams] at the moment of eclosion. This minute wet weight at birth is consistent with the small egg diameter of roughly 1.4 millimeters that characterizes the pelagic eggs of this species. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the mouth opens and the yolk sac is fully resorbed, at which point the larva must encounter suitable planktonic prey to avoid the point of no return. The short incubation period likely reflects the selective pressures of a warm, oligotrophic environment where rapid hatching can reduce vulnerability to predation on the egg stage.

The maximum reproductive output of Alepes djedaba has been quantified from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. At a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], a single ripe female can release as many as 640,800 eggs in one spawning event [N_R_i = 640,800 eggs in one spawning event], and the species is known to spawn approximately 365 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 times per year], indicating a nearly continuous reproductive strategy in tropical waters. This extraordinary fecundity is characteristic of many small to medium-sized carangids that produce pelagic eggs subject to high rates of planktonic mortality. The daily rate of egg production, while immense, must be viewed in the context of the low survival probability from the ichthyoplankton stage through to juvenile recruitment. Such high reproductive investment suggests that the species is adapted to a highly uncertain early-life environment where only a tiny fraction of offspring survive to settlement.

Around the time of puberty, individuals of Alepes djedaba have an estimated wet weight of 50.8 grams [Wwp = 50.8 grams], which corresponds well with the length at first maturation. The growth trajectory in this species is such that the ultimate wet weight reaches approximately 718 grams [Wwi = approximately 718 grams] by the time fish approach their maximum length. This represents a substantial increase in mass from the juvenile stage, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissue necessary for successful reproduction and long-term survival. The relationship between length and mass, derived from a large sample collected across the species' range, shows that body condition improves steadily with size until asymptotic mass is approached. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Alepes kleinii indicate that the shrimp scad achieves a slightly larger ultimate size, possibly due to differences in foraging ecology or habitat productivity in the regions it inhabits.

The maximum lifespan of Alepes djedaba under natural conditions has been estimated at 5 years [am = 5 years] based on otolith analyses of wild-caught specimens from the Arabian Sea, where the ambient water temperature averages 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of fast-growing, highly fecund tropical carangids that experience high natural mortality rates from piscivorous predators. The oldest documented individuals rarely exceed this age, suggesting that senescence and age-related physiological decline set in relatively early. In contrast, the age at birth, estimated at 6 days [ab = 6 days] under the same thermal regime, highlights the compressed early developmental phase of this species at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. The combination of rapid incubation, early maturity at a modest size, and continuous high fecundity throughout a short adult life defines a life-history strategy well suited to the variable and productive environments of warm coastal seas.
